summary: The note traces early geological thought to medieval Persian and Chinese scholars. It cites Fielding H. Garrison's view that the science's origin can be traced to Persia after the Muslim conquests. It then summarizes contributions by Abu al-Rayhan al-Biruni, Ibn Sina (Avicenna), and Shen Kuo, covering India's geology, mountain and earthquake explanations, and land formation through erosion and silt deposition.
one_line: Summarizes early geological contributions from Persian scholars Al-Biruni and Ibn Sina and Chinese polymath Shen Kuo.
key_facts: Some modern scholars, such as Fielding H. Garrison, hold that the origin of the science of geology can be traced to Persia after the Muslim conquests had come to an end.
Abu al-Rayhan al-Biruni (973–1048 CE) was one of the earliest Persian geologists.
Abu al-Rayhan al-Biruni's works included the earliest writings on the geology of India.
Abu al-Rayhan al-Biruni hypothesized that the Indian subcontinent was once a sea.
Ibn Sina (Avicenna, 981–1037) was a Persian scholar who drew from Greek and Indian scientific literature that were not destroyed by the Muslim conquests.
Ibn Sina proposed detailed explanations for the formation of mountains.
Ibn Sina proposed detailed explanations for the origin of earthquakes.
Ibn Sina's explanations provided an essential foundation for the later development of the science of geology.
Shen Kuo (1031–1095) was a Chinese polymath who formulated a hypothesis for the process of land formation.
Shen Kuo based his hypothesis on observing fossil animal shells in a geological stratum in a mountain hundreds of miles from the ocean.
Shen Kuo inferred that the land was formed by erosion of the mountains and by deposition of silt.
